claims.text: Cast refractory multi-principal element alloys such as Nb-Mo-Ta-W-V have limited ductility and may form brittle intermetallics during cooling.
The initial cast alloy has coarse grains larger than 10 µm.
Mechanical alloying for at least 40 hours produces a nanocrystalline or amorphous state.
Repeated cold welding and fracturing during mechanical alloying introduce high defect density and refine grains to the nanometer scale.
Spark plasma sintering at 900–1000 °C for less than 30 minutes suppresses grain growth and intermetallic precipitation while consolidating the powder.
Rapid SPS heating and cooling kinetically trap the nanocrystalline state.
Mechanical alloying can produce two BCC solid solutions in a refractory multi-principal element alloy powder.
SPS-consolidated NbMoTaWVTi can contain an FCC TiO precipitate introduced through oxygen contamination.
VEC below 6.87 and atomic size difference below 6.6% ensure thermodynamic stability of solid-solution phases.
Adjusting VEC to between 4.4 and 6.0 and maintaining δ below 6.6% stabilizes a dual-phase BCC+BCC or BCC+FCC solid-solution structure.
SPS at 1400 °C causes coarsening of the BCC grains.
Sintering mechanically alloyed refractory HEA powder can partially decompose a BCC solid solution into Laves phases.
The proposed MA/SPS route will produce a bulk alloy with an average grain size below 50 nm.
The proposed alloy will have yield strength above 2000 MPa.
The proposed alloy will have hardness above 600 Hv.
The proposed alloy will have ductility above 10% because its dual-phase solid-solution structure prevents brittle fracture.
The consolidated alloy will contain no detectable brittle intermetallic phases, including Laves phases or TiO.
The nanocrystalline dual-phase structure becomes unstable above an SPS temperature of 1100 °C.
VEC above 6.87 promotes a brittle BCC structure or intermetallic formation.
The cast baseline has yield strength of approximately 1000–1200 MPa and ductility below 5%.

contradictions.description: The proposed VEC window extends to 6.0 while predicting ductility above 10%, although the phase-stability evidence invoked in the hypothesis reports an empirical brittle-alloy regime beginning at VEC 4.6.

The boundary attributes potential Laves-phase formation to temperatures above 1100 °C and cites the 1400 °C study, but the cited study reports that increasing temperature to 1400 °C decreased rather than increased Laves-phase content.
